fields.name: Agriculture, veterinary and food
fields.governing_thought: Agriculture is divided by the level at which production is managed: the organism, the crop or herd, the farm enterprise, and the food and rural system.

sections.statement: The organism level covers what is grown or raised: breeding, genetics, biotechnology and the classes of plants and animals used as stock.
At the organism level, biotechnology analyses and engineers individual plants and animals and produces genetically modified stock.
At the organism level, living things used or met in production are classed by lineage, habitat, relationships and individual traits.
The crop and herd level covers how a population of plants or animals is kept productive: growing, husbandry, nutrition, and plant and animal health.
At the crop and herd level, growing crops, pastures, horticultural plants and trees depends on physiology, nutrition and agronomic management.
At the crop and herd level, livestock and fish populations are fed, bred, kept and managed through husbandry and aquaculture.
At the crop and herd level, plant and animal health protects populations against pathogens, pests, disease and environmental stress.
The farm level covers how one production unit is run: its inputs, operations, machinery, management, planning and farm economics.
At the farm level, inputs are the sites, materials, technologies and finance that a production unit starts from.
At the farm level, operations are the field and farm work through which a production unit establishes, grows and obtains its output.
At the farm level, management plans, monitors, protects and directs the production unit and handles its risks.
The food and rural system level covers what leaves the farm and how the sector is governed: harvest handling, products, residues, markets, policy and rural change.
At the food and rural system level, harvested output is handled, moved, processed and assured as safe food.
At the food and rural system level, products are the outputs that leave production, classed by origin, use and handling.
At the food and rural system level, residues are the by-products, wastes, released substances and digestive contents that remain after production.
At the food and rural system level, governance and rural change cover the institutions, policies, pressures and transitions shaping the sector.

fields.name: Arts and literature
fields.governing_thought: Arts and literature is divided by the feature of the work a claim is about, running outward from the material object to judgment: medium and making, form, meaning, context and reception, and value.
fields.note: Misplaced: P2.2.2.5 Literary theory (belongs in P3), P2.2.1.5 Print culture and P2.2.2.3 Comparative literature (P4), P4.3.3.1 Ecocriticism (P3), P4.3.1.4 agriculture/food/wine, P4.2.1.2 Asian cultural studies.

sections.statement: Medium and making is the feature of a work concerned with the material, technique and process by which it is produced.
Medium and making in visual and material art concerns works produced by shaping physical materials with hand, tool or lens.
Medium and making in screen and digital media concerns works produced with cameras, computers and interactive technologies.
Medium and making in performance concerns works produced live through the bodies and actions of performers.
Medium and making in writing concerns works produced by composing text for creative, digital, site-based or professional purposes.
Medium and making in music concerns works produced as organised sound through composition, performance and recording.
Form is the feature of a work concerned with its design, structure, genre and style as it appears to the audience.
Form in visual works is the arrangement of design elements, colour and visible effects that an audience perceives.
Form in texts is the genre and type of writing that shapes how a written work appears to its readers.
Meaning is the feature of a work concerned with what it represents, expresses and conveys through ideas and theory.
Meaning is explained by theoretical approaches that account for how visual art and cultural images produce significance.
Meaning is carried by the ideas, themes and values that culture associates with works and that the works themselves convey.
Context and reception is the feature of a work concerned with the place, language, time, industry and audience in which it is produced and received.
Context and reception by place and language groups literary works according to the region or tongue in which they were written.
Context and reception through cultural place and movement concerns how works arise from regions, migration and colonial encounter.
Context and reception through industry and audience concerns how works are produced, distributed, consumed and read.
Value is the feature of a work concerned with how it is judged, studied historically and assigned standing within culture.
Value in visual art is assigned through its history and through critical judgment of individual works.
Value in screen and performance is assigned through scholarly study and criticism of films, theatre and dance.
Value in music is assigned through scholarly, historical and critical writing about musical works and traditions.

fields.name: Biology
fields.governing_thought: Biological claims are divided by the level or process they concern, running from the copied sequence to the interacting community: heritable information, the cell, the organism, descent, and ecological interaction.

sections.statement: Heritable information is the level at which claims concern copied sequences, genes, genomes and the molecules that carry them.
Sequence analysis and nucleic acid chemistry address claims about the sequences, tools and molecular classes that make up genetic material.
Genetics fields address claims about how heritable information operates in cell division, development, genomes and research traditions.
The cell is the level at which claims concern biomolecules, cellular processes, signals and the materials cells make.
Molecular and cellular processes cover how biomolecules and cells function, grow, communicate and transport material.
Amino acids, peptides and proteins are the molecules from which cells build their machinery.
Signalling and regulatory molecules are substances that carry messages or control cellular and immune activity.
Cell-derived materials and cellular physiology cover substances obtained from cells and the metabolic and cell-physiological processes they perform.
The organism is the level at which claims concern the body structures, physiology, behaviour and kinds of whole living individuals.
Body structures are the anatomical parts and regions of the organism, from general anatomy to musculoskeletal and digestive systems.
Organ systems and body products are the specific systems, tissues and structures that carry out bodily functions in animals, plants and microbes.
Physiology and behaviour concern how whole organisms function, develop, behave and fall ill.
Kinds of organism are the taxa and whole-organism fields that study particular groups of living things.
Descent is the process by which claims concern how lineages are related, adapt, split and vanish over evolutionary time.
Systematics and general evolutionary biology name, classify and reconstruct the relationships of organisms across the branches of life.
Evolutionary change concerns adaptation, developmental evolution and life histories shaped over generations.
Lineage patterns concern how lineages are distributed in space and time, split into species and disappear.
Ecological interaction is the level at which claims concern organisms relating to each other, to habitats and to the wider environment.
Ecology subfields address interactions at the level of behaviour, populations, communities and habitats.
Interactions between species and the changing environment concern hosts, parasites, climate, whole-animal adaptation and industrial uses of organisms.
Environmental mixtures and forensic work concern natural, waste and polluting materials and the biological evidence found in them.

fields.name: Business, trade, tax and accounting
fields.governing_thought: Business divides by the practice of the firm, running from the record outward to customers and borders, into accounts, finance, operations and organisation, marketing, and trade and tax.
fields.note: Misplaced: P1.1.1 and P1.2.1 (core accounting under context-specific), P2.3.2 (insurance under asset-holding), P3.3.2.3 (valuation), P5.1.2.3 (retail under wholesale), P3.3.3.

sections.statement: Accounts is the practice of the firm in which financial information is recorded, reported, audited and made accountable.
Context-specific accounting adapts the firm's record keeping to cross-border, non-profit and sustainability settings.
Auditing and core accounting cover the checking of a firm's records and the methods by which they are kept and reported.
Finance is the practice of the firm in which funds, credit, investment and risk are raised, held, exchanged and insured.
Finance research fields study how financial institutions, flows, insurance and investment operate and are applied.
The financial industry is made up of the kinds of firm that intermediate money, trade securities and bear risk.
Asset-holding firms provide access to funds, property and rented or leased assets.
Operations and organisation is the practice of the firm in which goods and services are produced, delivered and managed.
Production operations make physical goods and supply utilities by transforming raw and intermediate materials.
Service operations move, hold, inform, support and care for people, businesses and society.
Organisation covers how firms are directed, staffed, governed and run, including commercial service management and health care organisation.
Marketing is the practice of the firm in which offerings are understood, priced, promoted and delivered to customers, including tourism and hospitality.
Core marketing covers the functions, market-specific forms and supporting tools through which a firm reaches its market.
Tourism marketing and management cover how firms manage, forecast and assess tourism and visitors.
Hospitality firms serve visitors with lodging and meals.
Trade and tax is the practice of the firm in which goods are bought and resold across markets and borders, with the commercial dealings that carry the firm's tax and trading obligations.
Commerce and wholesale trade cover firms that resell goods to other businesses by kind of customer and merchant.
Vehicle trade covers firms that sell, service and fuel motor vehicles.
Retail trade covers stores that sell goods directly to consumers.

fields.name: Chemistry
fields.governing_thought: Chemistry's objects divide by the question asked of a substance into its composition and identity, its structure and bonding, its equilibrium and energy, its rates and mechanisms, and its synthesis and analysis.
fields.note: Key line holds; worst misplaced: P5.1.1 (biological macromolecules) belongs under P1.4, P5.1.2.1 and P5.1.2.4 under P4, and P1.5.1.4 under P1.4.

sections.statement: Composition and identity is the question of what a substance is, covering its general kind, role and chemical or biological class.
General entities and roles name the broad kinds of chemical object and the functions they play.
Inorganic and organometallic classes identify substances by the elements and metal centres from which they are composed.
Organic and ring-based classes identify substances by their carbon frameworks.
Biological classes identify substances by their biochemical nature as macromolecules, enzymes, hormones and nutrients.
Medicinal and biomolecular classes identify substances by their biological activity and their use in medicine.
Structure and bonding is the question of how a substance is built, how its parts attract one another and what measurable properties follow.
Condensed and extended structures ask how atoms and molecules are assembled into solids, frameworks and materials.
Interactions and structural probes ask how molecules attract one another and how their arrangement is revealed.
Measured properties and their theory ask what quantities and responses a substance displays and how they are computed.
Equilibrium and energy is the question of how a substance settles into states, exchanges matter and energy and moves between phases.
Energetics and solution states ask how energy, charge and solvent govern a substance at equilibrium.
Phase and state changes ask how a substance separates, converts or deteriorates into another condition.
Interfaces, barriers and gradients ask how a substance crosses, exchanges across or is held at a boundary.
Rates and mechanisms is the question of how fast a substance changes and by what steps its bonds are rearranged.
Kinetics and catalysis ask how fast and by what route a reaction proceeds.
Specific reaction types ask how particular driving conditions or bond changes transform a substance.
Synthesis and analysis is the question of how a substance is made, isolated, detected and measured.
Synthetic and organic approaches ask how substances are built and what they are used for.
Analytical methods ask how a substance is identified and quantified by instruments and spectra.
Separation and sensing ask how components are isolated and detected in mixtures and forensic or residual cases.

fields.name: Computer science
fields.governing_thought: Computer science is divided by the property asserted of a computation, running from the single program outward to many agents and adversaries: correctness, cost, coordination, learning and protection.
fields.note: Worst misplacements: P2.2.2 Virtual machine monitors, P2.1.2 cryptography, P2.3.2.3 Technology acceptance model, P3.2.2.1 Networking, P3.3.1.5 Evolutionary computation, P5.3.2.3 Mixed initiative, P4.2.2.2 Data systems.

sections.statement: Correctness is the property that a computation meets its specification, shown through formal theory, mathematical foundations, verification and sound software construction.
Theoretical foundations assert that a computation has provable, mathematically describable properties and defined expressive power.
Numerical and mathematical software and coding operations assert that a computation represents and approximates quantities accurately and recovers messages without error.
Software engineering asserts that programs are specified, built, tested and maintained so that they behave as intended.
Cost is the property of how much time, energy, space or information a computation consumes, and how that consumption is measured and traded off.
Algorithmic and computational cost asserts how hard a computation is in principle and how it is designed to be efficient.
System performance asserts how fast, how parallel and how energy-frugal a running computation is, and how well it chooses among alternatives.
Information cost asserts how many symbols a message needs, measured by entropy, distance and rate-distortion limits and extended to coding in networks.
Coordination is the property of how a computation works with other components, machines, agents and people through shared structure and interaction.
Networks and distributed execution assert that many machines cooperate through shared structures, rules and concurrent execution.
Deployed platforms assert that computation is delivered across clouds, mobile devices, services and physical systems.
Agents and people assert that a computation interacts with other agents and users through robotics, interfaces and applications.
Media and creative computing asserts that a computation generates, transforms and presents content for human audiences.
Learning is the property that a computation improves or exhibits intelligent behaviour from data, experience and reasoning rather than fixed rules.
Machine learning asserts that behaviour is acquired from data under supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement and adversarial regimes.
Perception and pattern learning asserts that a computation interprets language, images and signals by recognising patterns in them.
Artificial and computational intelligence asserts that a computation reasons, evolves and develops intelligently.
Protection is the property that a computation resists attack, keeps information confidential and can be trusted by the people it affects.
Formal and data-centred protection asserts provable secrecy, integrity and privacy of information handled by a computation.
System protection asserts that hardware, software and networks resist attack and fail detectably.
Human and policy protection asserts that people, regulation and trust properties such as fairness and oversight constrain a computation.

fields.name: Design and the built environment
fields.governing_thought: Design's objects divide, from need to outcome, into five aspects of a designed arrangement for human use: use and need, form, performance in use, place and settlement, and the life of the built thing.
fields.note: Misplaced: P5.1.1, P5.1.3 and P5.1.4 (generic design practice under life of built thing), P5.3.2.3 design management, P1.2.5 home economics.

sections.statement: Use and need is the aspect of design concerned with the people, purposes, activities and problems that a designed arrangement must answer.
Activities, functions and events are the human doings and purposes that call for a designed arrangement.
Human-centred and social design responds to the people, experiences and services that a design is made for.
Community needs identify the shared goals and voices of the people for whom places and things are designed.
Form is the aspect of design concerned with the shape, material make-up and style of designed objects, spaces and images.
Designed objects and their parts are the artefacts, components and furnishings that take a definite physical shape.
Designed spaces, images and their styles give shape to interiors, buildings and visual messages.
Computational modelling of form uses digital methods to generate, visualise and test design shapes before they are made.
Performance in use is the aspect of design concerned with how well a designed arrangement behaves for its users, in safety, comfort, energy and resilience.
Human safety and comfort in design covers how designs fit the body and protect people from harm.
Environmental and technical performance covers the scientific and sustainability measures of how buildings and designs work.
Place and settlement is the aspect of design concerned with arranging sites, cities, regions and the land and services they depend on.
Planning of land, regions and systems sets the strategic and regulatory frame for where and how settlement grows.
Urban and regional analysis studies the housing, economies and data of settlements to understand how places function.
Design of places and landscapes gives physical shape to cities, open spaces and the wider built environment.
Life of the built thing is the aspect of design concerned with how buildings are practised, constructed, managed, conserved and understood over time.
Design practice and its disciplines cover the general methods and processes by which designers work from first idea to finished work.
Construction and its technology cover the building of a structure and the tools and systems used to make it.
Management and economics of building cover the organisation, costing and running of design and construction work.
History, heritage and theory record and interpret how designed and built things were made, valued and conserved.

fields.name: Earth: geography and geology
fields.governing_thought: Earth science claims are divided by what the claim is about, running from rock to settlement: materials, internal motion, deep time, surface and fluid envelopes, and human spatial organization.
fields.note: Misplaced: P5.3.2.2 and P5.3.2.3 (models, belong in method line), P5.3.1 versus P3.2.3.1 (natural hazards), P1.2.1.1 (duplicate geochemistry), P2.3.3 (applied geophysics).

sections.statement: Materials are what the Earth is made of, namely the chemistry, minerals, rocks and fluids that compose it.
Materials at the chemical level are the elements, isotopes and reactions that make up earth substances, including those built by organisms.
Materials at the mineral and rock level are the crystals, rocks, fluids and ore bodies whose composition and properties define the solid Earth.
Internal motion is the force, field and movement within the solid Earth that deforms, heats and shakes it.
Internal motion appears as heat flow, deformation, faulting and magma rising through the crust and mantle of the solid Earth.
Internal motion shapes the Earth's figure, gravity and magnetic field, which record how mass and molten metal move within the planet.
Internal motion is probed through seismic waves and electrical currents that reveal structure and movement beneath the surface.
Deep time is the history of the Earth, covering the age, layering, life and climate records preserved in its materials.
Deep time is read in the dated layers of sediment and the fossils they hold, which together order Earth history.
Deep time includes past climates and environments, reconstructed from ice, land, ocean and lake archives.
Surface and fluid envelopes are the land surface, ice, waters and air that wrap the solid Earth, together with the means of observing them.
Surface and fluid envelopes begin at the land surface, where landforms, frozen ground, soils and surface temperature form and change.
Surface and fluid envelopes include the waters of the land and the sea, their motion, heat, properties and seabed.
Surface and fluid envelopes end in the air and the climate system it carries, from atmospheric composition and weather to long-term climate change.
Human spatial organization is how people locate, map, settle, use and manage places, and how they organize information about them.
Human spatial organization starts with locating and mapping places, naming regions, drawing boundaries and holding place data in geographic systems.
Human spatial organization covers how societies settle and live in places and how they shape and respond to their environments.
Human spatial organization includes managing places against natural hazards by mapping risk, preparing responses and issuing warnings.

fields.name: Economics
fields.governing_thought: Economics is divided by who settles an allocation: individuals and households, firms and markets, governments and public institutions, and the economy as a whole.
fields.note: Worst misplaced: P2.2.3.4 antitrust, P3.1.4.2 industry studies, P4.3.1 macro behavioral, P4.3.5.1 spatial economics, P4.1.5.3 labor, P2.4.4.1 household analysis.

sections.statement: Individuals and households settle allocations through their own choices about consumption, work, learning, health and risk.
Individuals settle allocations through their own choices under information limits, uncertainty and behavioral bias.
Households settle allocations through family decisions on saving, finance and demographic composition.
Individuals and communities settle allocations through their work, schooling, health and wellbeing decisions.
Firms and markets settle allocations through production, exchange, pricing and competition in labour, product, financial, land and resource markets.
Firms settle allocations through production, organization, business administration, accounting and personnel decisions.
Markets settle allocations through pricing, market structure, competition and the matching of workers and employers.
Financial markets and network systems settle allocations through trading, intermediation, transport and communication.
Industries, land and natural resources settle allocations through sector markets and the use of places and resources.
Specific industries settle allocations through their own market conditions in agriculture, tourism, transport and industrial organisation.
Governments and public institutions settle allocations through law, regulation, taxation, public choice and the redistribution of welfare.
Governments settle allocations through law, legal procedure and regulation of business conduct.
Governments settle allocations through public provision, taxation and local or intergovernmental arrangements.
Public institutions settle allocations through welfare assessment, collective decision-making and community development.
The whole economy settles allocations in aggregate through money, prices, growth, development and trade between countries.
The whole economy settles allocations in aggregate through output, money, prices and policy.
Whole countries settle allocations through development, growth and the structure of their economic systems.
Trade between countries settles allocations across borders through exchange, factor movement and aggregate behavior.
The whole economy's history shows allocations settled over time through the aggregate and sector records of economic history.

fields.name: Education
fields.governing_thought: Education is divided by the element of an educational arrangement, running from purpose to system: aims and curricula, learners, teaching, assessment, and institutions and systems.
fields.note: Misplaced: P1.2.3.1 (activities under curricula), P4.5.2.2, P4.4.1/P4.4.2 (evaluation types apart from P4.3), P3.1.2.3, P3.3.3.4, P5.4.2.2, P3.1.3.3.

sections.statement: Aims and curricula are the element of an educational arrangement that sets what is to be learned, through subject content, programs, frameworks and the perspectives that frame them.
Subject and language content are the disciplines, languages and applied fields that learners are taught as the substance of instruction.
Programs and curriculum designs are the organized offerings, specialized fields and course structures through which content is packaged for learners.
Frameworks and perspectives are the theoretical, civic, policy and cultural lenses that frame what education aims to do.
Curriculum planning and organizing approaches are the methods, designs and outcomes through which a curriculum is planned and framed.
Learners are the element of an educational arrangement that consists of the people taught, their inner attributes, circumstances, social background and the support they receive.
Learner-internal elements are the minds, traits, capacities and behaviours that a learner brings to and enacts within education.
Learner circumstances and health are the conditions, needs, health states and hazards that shape a learner's situation.
Learner social background is the family, peer and life circumstance that acts on a learner from outside instruction.
Learner support and progression are the helpers, services, care and pathways through which others assist the learner and the learner advances.
Teaching is the element of an educational arrangement that carries instruction out, through methods, organization, materials, and enrichment or remediation.
Instructional organization and methods are the ways teaching is arranged, grouped and delivered in practice.
Instructional materials and activities are the prepared content, simulations and tasks through which students are actually taught.
Enrichment, diagnosis and remediation are the adjustments and supports that extend or correct the standard curriculum to fit learners' needs.
Assessment is the element of an educational arrangement that judges learning and instruction, through measurement concepts, instruments, evaluation practice and research method.
Tests and test use are the instruments, their design, administration and scoring through which learning is measured.
Learner measures are the ratings, inventories and predictive indicators that capture what students achieve, know, feel or may do.
Evaluation concepts and practice are the field-level ideas, approaches, issues and methods of judging learners, courses and programs.
Evaluation types and records are the vocational, writing, alternative and written-record forms through which results are judged and documented.
Research and statistical methods are the observational, comparative, experimental and statistical procedures used to gather and analyse evidence about education.

Institutions and systems are the element of an educational arrangement that organizes, governs, resources and connects education to society, through governance, resources, finance and work and society links.
Governance and administration are the leaders, rules, staffing and control mechanisms through which institutions are directed and held accountable.
Organizational form and program structure are the lifecycle stages, sector arrangements and change processes defining how education is organized.
Law, equity, policy and community context are the courts, democratic values, governmental and cultural conditions that regulate and surround education.
Resources and provision are the places, equipment, media, materials and programs that institutions rely on to deliver and document education.
Funding, work and community links are the money, economic conditions, labour and social surroundings that sustain institutions and tie them to society.

fields.name: Engineering
fields.governing_thought: Engineering is divided by the kind of system the engineer designs: materials and the making of things, structures, machines and vehicles, energy and process systems, and electrical, information and control systems.
fields.note: Misplaced: P3.1.1.4 Maritime engineering (belongs P2.3), P1.3.3.1 and P1.3.3.2 (belong P1.4), P1.5.2.1 Nanophotonics (duplicates P1.4.1.3), P3.3.1.3 Particle physics.

sections.statement: Materials and manufacturing systems are designed to make artefacts: material classes, nanostructures, fabrication and production processes.
Manufacturing systems are designed production routes, tools and organisation that turn material into finished artefacts.
Materials systems are designed classes of matter, from atoms and compounds to structural and functional materials, whose properties set artefact performance.
Insulation and packaging systems are designed insulating media and component enclosures that protect and bound electrical artefacts.
Nanoscale device systems are designed devices and nanomaterials built from nanometre-sized structures, with their electronic and constitutive behaviour.
Nanoscale making systems are designed fabrication, assembly and measurement routes that produce nanostructures and fix their optical, fluidic and geometric behaviour.
Structures, machines and vehicles are designed systems whose behaviour is set by force and motion, from aircraft and ships to mechanisms and precision devices.
Aerospace vehicles are designed flying systems whose behaviour is set by lift, thrust, weight and structural force balance.
Road vehicles are designed ground systems whose behaviour is set by powertrain, crash, guidance and propulsion forces.
Marine craft and platforms are designed floating systems whose behaviour is set by buoyancy, hydrodynamic load and structural balance.
Robotic machines are designed self-acting systems whose behaviour is set by actuation and task-level force and motion.
Civil structures are designed fixed systems whose behaviour is set by loads, ground conditions and earthquake shaking.
Energy, fluid and process systems are designed to convert energy or move and transform matter, as in power plants, heat systems, chemical and environmental processes and resource extraction.
Fluid systems are designed to move fluid and carry its forces, from external flows and living fluids to computed and fundamental flows.
Energy and radiation systems are designed to generate, convert and control energy, plasma, particle beams and radiation.
Particulate and nuclear device systems are designed to handle grains, particles and radiation through momentum and balance laws.
Chemical, environmental and resource process systems are designed to react, separate, treat, extract and manage matter and its environmental burden.
Electrical, information and control systems are designed to carry charge, signals and decisions, from circuits and electromagnetics to communications, sensing, robotics and control.
Electrical and device systems are designed to carry charge and field through components, magnetic artefacts and semiconductor devices.
Communication and signal systems are designed to carry, shape and process information-bearing signals.
Sensing, control and autonomous systems are designed to measure the world and act on it through transducers, imaging, instrumentation, feedback and robotics.
Control and systems-behaviour concepts are designed to steer organised systems and return measured behaviour to a target.

fields.name: Environmental science
fields.governing_thought: Environmental science places each coupled human–environment claim on one link of the causal chain: pressure, state, impact, response, or limit.

sections.statement: Pressures are the loads that human activity places on the environment.
Emissions are the loads from greenhouse gases and other pollutants.
Land and sea use changes are the loads from clearance, drainage, and building.
Extraction is the load from taking water, minerals, or living stocks.
Introduced species are the loads from pests and organisms people bring in.
Drivers are the activities that create a load, grouped here because the load is the pressure.
States are the measured conditions of air, water, soil, and living systems.
Measured conditions are the states of air, water, soil, and living systems.
Natural hazards and processes are geological, weather, and ecological events.
Natural resources are stocks of water, minerals, energy, and living systems.
Impacts are the harms a changed state causes, and the way those harms are attributed.
Ecosystem harm is the loss of function or species after a changed state.
Human health impact is the harm to people that follows an exposure.
Responses are the actions taken to change a pressure or a state.
Restoration is the response that aims at measured recovery.
Conservation is the response that protects areas and cuts pressures on them.
Regulation is the response whose environmental effect is what this field measures.
Environmental engineering is the technical work that changes a pressure or a state.
Limits are the thresholds a measured state is not meant to cross.
Thresholds are the critical values past which a system shifts.
Standards are the agreed limits a measured state is held to.
Carrying capacity is the limit of what a system can sustain.

fields.name: History
fields.governing_thought: History's objects divide by what a sentence asserts about the human past, running from the single fact to its meaning: occurrence, time, cause, change and continuity, and meaning and memory.
fields.note: Archaeological sociology (P1.2.1.4), History of religion (P3.2.5), Historical periods (P4.3.1.2) and era histories P2.2.1-P2.2.2 sit awkwardly.

sections.statement: Occurrence is the assertion that something happened, established from the material, written and personal evidence the past left behind.
Archaeological evidence establishes that past events occurred by recovering sites, objects, remains and their context from the ground and water.
Archaeologies of particular settings assert occurrence through the traces left in industrial, maritime, bodily and regional contexts.
Documentary and emblematic records assert occurrence through inscriptions, coins, lives, lineages and signs of identity.
Time is the assertion that events belong to a particular moment, ordered by calendars and divided into eras.
Chronology and the broad periods of the past assert when things happened by fixing dates and dividing time into eras.
Era histories assert that the past divides into medieval, classical and contemporary periods, each with its own character.
Cause is the assertion that events happened because of political, social, imperial or other human forces that shaped them.
Political and imperial histories assert that power, states and empires drove what happened.
Social and thematic histories assert that collective structures, group identities and particular human concerns caused historical outcomes.
Change and continuity is the assertion that peoples, states and the human past as a whole persisted or were transformed over time, within places and across borders.
Histories of peoples and states assert how particular nations and regions persisted and were transformed, in Europe and beyond it.
Histories of movement and connection assert that change came through migration, exchange and relations that crossed borders.
Histories of civilization as a whole assert continuity and transformation across the entire human past rather than within one nation or region.
Meaning and memory is the assertion that the past matters through how it is remembered, interpreted, kept and passed on.
Historical thought and method assert how the past should be understood, researched and reflected on.
Collective memory and myth assert that communities hold stories of the past that give it shared meaning.
Archives, museums and collections assert that the past is preserved and interpreted through the institutions that keep its records and objects.
Heritage management and conservation assert that the past is protected, managed and passed on, physically and digitally, to living audiences.

fields.name: Indigenous knowledge
fields.governing_thought: Indigenous knowledge is divided by the aspect of a knowledge system a claim is about, running from its ordering principles through its relations to land and waters, its governance and custom, and its transmission to its research and data.
fields.note: Misplaced: P1.2.4.1 and P1.2.5.2/P1.2.5.3 (land, expression and education under ordering principles), P3.1.1.1, P3.3.3.3, P5.1.3.1 (health model under research).

sections.statement: Ordering principles are the way an Indigenous knowledge system organises what is known, through its sciences, philosophies, worldviews and the technologies and innovations it generates.
Whole science traditions and their subject areas are the bodies of natural-world knowledge that each Indigenous people holds as a complete system.
Philosophy, religion and ways of knowing, being and doing are the worldviews and values that ground Indigenous knowledge.
Technology and innovation fields are the engineered, computed and newly created things that Indigenous knowledge produces.
Relations to land and waters are the aspect of Indigenous knowledge concerned with how peoples know, use, conserve and manage country, sea and living things.
Environmental knowledges are the broad fields through which each Indigenous people understands and manages its environment.
Land-based practice covers farming, forestry, earth science, conservation and land and water management carried out on country.
Marine and fisheries knowledge covers customary fishing and the science of the sea within Indigenous systems.
Pacific orientation fields distinguish knowing the environment from actively conserving and harvesting its resources.
Governance and custom are the aspect of Indigenous knowledge concerned with how communities are ruled, how roles and rights are defined, and how health and wellbeing are cared for.
Law, politics, economy and planning are the structures through which Indigenous rights, land and wealth are governed.
Information and knowledge governance covers how Indigenous knowledge and data are held, managed and controlled.
Peoples, roles and professional practice are the communities who hold the knowledge and the enterprise and social work done for them.
Health and wellbeing care covers the cultural determinants, science, services and policy through which Indigenous health is sustained.
Transmission is the aspect of Indigenous knowledge concerned with how it is taught, spoken, written, preserved and handed on to new generations.
Education at each stage and sector is where Indigenous knowledge is formally handed on to learners.
Language, history and creative expression are the spoken, written and performed media that carry Indigenous knowledge across time.
Heritage and taonga are the material objects and collections through which Indigenous knowledge is preserved and returned.
Research and data are the aspect of Indigenous knowledge concerned with the methods, data technologies and global studies through which it is investigated and governed by outside research.
Methods and data are the research approaches and information technologies used to generate and govern Indigenous knowledge.
Global Indigenous studies are the cross-peoples fields that examine Indigenous culture, environment, health, society and science together.

fields.name: Information and the record
fields.governing_thought: Information science is divided by the stage in the life of a record, from creation to keeping: creation and publication, description, arrangement, retrieval and use, and preservation and governance.
fields.note: Misplaced: P3.4.5.3 (description stage) belongs under P2; P3.4.2.4 and P3.4.2.5 belong under P3.2/P3.3; P5.2.2.3 (OPACs) belongs under P4; P2.2.2.3 retrieval tools.

sections.statement: Creation and publication is the stage in which records come into being, are produced and are issued to their audiences.
Creation and publication begins with documentary origination, in which writing, knowledge and broadcast sources first become primary records.
Creation and publication also includes data capture, in which streams, sensors, graphs and media are gathered and extracted into records.
Creation and publication continues with production and dissemination, in which records are printed, reproduced, published and circulated to readers.
Creation and publication ends in published forms, the formats, components and study characteristics that issued records take.
Description is the stage in which a record is named, listed and indexed so that its content and subject are represented.
Description starts with subject and content analysis, which determines what a record is about and how its terms are named.
Description through indexing represents a record's subject by index terms, citation links and controlled indexing languages.
Description through bibliographic recording sets down the elements of each item under rules and gathers them into lists.
Arrangement is the stage in which described records are ordered into classes by classification systems, theory and control structures.
Arrangement rests on classification theory, the philosophical origins and organizing principles by which knowledge is divided into classes.
Arrangement by general schemes orders the whole of recorded knowledge for libraries and the book trade.
Arrangement by domain schemes orders the records and phenomena of a single field of research or practice.
Arrangement by control structures selects, standardizes and organizes records within collections so that their order is governed.
Retrieval and use is the stage in which arranged records are stored, searched for, found and used by their readers.
Retrieval and use depends on storage systems and databases that hold records so they can be searched.
Retrieval and use proceeds through searching, in which queries are run against sources and results are judged.
Retrieval and use by people covers how readers gain access to records and how they seek and interpret them.
Retrieval and use by computation turns retrieved records into applications, models and knowledge through systems and algorithms.
Preservation and governance is the final stage in which records are kept, protected and managed over the long term.
Preservation and governance requires holding institutions, the archives and libraries established with facilities and staff to keep records.
Preservation and governance through custody and curation keeps deposited records and data intact, accurate and accessible.
Preservation and governance through management and policy regulates how records are administered, protected and kept across their lifecycle.

fields.name: Law
fields.governing_thought: Law is divided by the legal relation a claim states, into sources, obligations, wrongs and remedies, public power, and forums and proof, running from where a rule gets its validity to how a dispute is decided.
fields.note: Misplaced: P1.2.1.4 Periodicals, P3.1.2.3 Tort law, P4.2.1.3 international human rights, P1.4.4 EU law, P1.5.3 space/aviation law, P2.1.1.3 Cyberspace law, P2.4.1.3 Americas law.

sections.statement: Sources are the relation in which a legal rule gains its validity through making, reform, theory or the norms binding states.
Law-making and reform concern how legal rules originate, change and develop over time.
Theory and setting of law state what law is and how it sits within society, science and thought.
International norms state the relations among states and the customary and treaty rules that bind them.
Comparative and cross-border law states how separate legal orders differ and how their rules meet.
Law of shared spaces and trade states the rules for seas, space, air and cross-border commerce.
Obligations are the relation in which persons owe duties and hold rights against one another in ownership, contract, status, trade and resource use.
Private relations state rights and duties between private parties through civil, contract, equity and property rules.
Commercial and work relations state the duties arising in business, finance, employment, tax and associations.
Personal standing states the rights and duties attached to a person's family, identity, nationality and status.
Domain-specific law states the duties arising from a particular area of social, technological or territorial life.
Resource duties state what the law requires of people regarding nature, animals, energy and natural resources.
Wrongs and remedies are the relation in which a party answers for harm through liability, punishment or settlement.
Liability states who is answerable for harm, including the state and private wrongdoers.
Criminal law states the public wrong between the state and an offender, at home and before international tribunals.
Studies of offending explain the kinds and causes of crime and who is labelled criminal.
Responses to wrong state how harm is sanctioned, punished or settled after it occurs.
Public power is the relation in which the state holds and exercises authority over persons and owes them protections.
Constitutional and administrative law state how public authority is structured and limited.
Rights and entitlements state what persons may claim from the state, from immunities to benefits and status.
Control and enforcement state how the state and its agents police and monitor conduct.
Forums and proof are the relation in which a claim is brought before an institution and decided by set procedure.
Deciding institutions are the courts, tribunals and arbitral bodies that apply law to disputing parties.
Procedure and claim-pursuit state the steps and means by which parties bring and resolve a case.
The legal profession and its training state who conducts cases and how they are prepared.

fields.name: Language
fields.governing_thought: Language divides into five aspects of its own: the signal that carries it, its form, its meaning, its variation in use, and the diversity of its languages and families.
fields.note: Worst misplaced: P4.2 and P4.3 media/communication studies, P4.1.4 translation under variation, P3.3 generic leftovers, and North American or South Asian groups under African or Pacific P5 sections.

sections.statement: Signal is the aspect of language concerned with the physical sounds and written marks that carry it.
Phonetics, the broader linguistics and speech field, and speech science are related kinds of study of the sound aspect of language.
Writing and script systems are the visual and symbolic means by which language is recorded in written or tactile form.
Form is the aspect of language concerned with its internal structure and the scholarly means used to describe it.
Grammar, vocabularies, sign systems and written conventions are the internal structure of a language.
Linguistic scholarship and its data-driven methods are the means by which the form of language is analysed and recorded.
Meaning is the aspect of language concerned with what words and sentences express and how that is recorded and used in context.
Fields concerned with the meaning of words and sentences study what language expresses and how those meanings are described.
Fields concerned with recording words and with language in context study how language is documented and used in practice.
This group covers specialised vocabulary and the general or uncategorised study of language and philology.
Variation in use is the aspect of language concerned with how it differs and is shared among people, across communities and through media.
Social use covers how language varies with social groups, is learned, and is carried between languages.
Media and communication studies cover the technologies, industries and institutions through which language is used publicly.
Communication studies cover environmental, international, organisational and interpersonal uses of language.
Diversity is the aspect of language concerned with the many languages and families of the world, grouped by kind and region.
General, contact and broad regional groupings collect languages by type or by wide areas rather than narrow descent.
Eurasian and Asian families are genealogical units of languages spoken from Europe and Siberia to East and South Asia.
African families are genealogical units of languages spoken across West, Central, East and southern Africa.
American families are genealogical units of indigenous languages of North, Central and South America.
Australian, Papuan and Pacific families are genealogical units of languages of Australia, New Guinea and the Pacific.

fields.name: Mathematics
fields.governing_thought: Mathematics is divided by the kind of question it asks, into algebraic and discrete structure, space and shape, change and the continuum, foundations and the discipline as a human activity, and the modelling of claims from other fields, in that order.
fields.note: Misplaced: P5.5.1 applied mathematics (generic), P5.5.2 numerical analysis (fits P3), P2.3.1 group theory (fits P1 structure).

sections.statement: Structure is the kind of question about operations, order, counting and number, and its topics study algebraic and discrete systems.
Algebraic systems study sets with operations such as fields, rings and algebras.
Discrete structure studies counting, order and the properties of whole numbers.
Linear and unifying structure studies matrices and the abstract languages of categories and K-theory that relate algebraic systems.
Space is the kind of question about shape, position and symmetry, and its topics study topology, geometry and groups.
Topology and manifolds study qualitative properties of space that survive continuous deformation.
Geometry studies measured, convex and algebraic shape in its classical and modern forms.
Symmetry studies the groups, including topological and Lie groups, that describe the symmetries of spaces.
Change and the continuum is the kind of question about limits, variation and functions, and its topics study analysis and the equations of change.
Real and classical analysis studies functions, measure, series and approximation on the real line.
Complex analysis studies functions of complex variables together with potentials and special functions.
Harmonic analysis and transforms study the decomposition of functions into oscillating components and the transforms that achieve it.
Equations and dynamics study how quantities evolve, through differential, difference and integral equations and dynamical systems.
Abstract analysis and optimisation study infinite-dimensional spaces, operators and extremal problems.
Foundations and the discipline is the kind of question about what mathematics rests on and how it is practised as a human activity, covering logic, history and teaching.
Mathematical logic and foundations
History and biography
Mathematics education
Proof and the foundations of mathematics ask what a valid proof is and what axioms mathematics rests on.
Modelling other fields is the kind of question about how mathematics expresses and computes claims from physics, decision science, biology, data and computing.
Physical modelling expresses claims about matter, fields and the cosmos in mathematical form.
Thermal, quantum and cosmic modelling expresses claims about heat, microscopic matter, gravity, stars and the earth.
Decision and living-systems modelling uses mathematics for choices, economies, biology and the earth.
Information and chance modelling uses mathematics for control, communication and random processes.
Computation applies mathematics to calculating answers and to the theory of computing.

fields.name: Medicine and the drug
fields.governing_thought: Medicine's knowledge is divided by the clinical question asked of a disorder, in the order of the clinical sequence: the disorders themselves, their causes and mechanisms, their diagnosis and prognosis, their treatment and drugs, and the populations and prevention in which they are met.
fields.note: Worst misplaced: P2.5.1 and P2.5.2 specialties (Psychiatry, Rheumatology, Endocrinology), P2.3.5, P3.2.2, P3.1.2, P4.5.1.1-3 nursing items and P5.4.3 sports science.

sections.statement: Disorders are the clinical question of what the condition is, grouped by the organ system, regulatory process, mental function or external cause affected.
Organ-system disorders are conditions defined by which organ, tissue or sensory system is affected and by the specialties that manage them.
Regulatory disorders are conditions in which a body regulatory process such as metabolism, hormones or immunity has failed.
Mental disorders are conditions that disturb mood, thought, cognition, drives or basic behaviours.
Infectious, neoplastic and externally caused disorders are conditions defined by the kind of insult that produces them.
Injury and animal diseases are disorders arising from physical trauma or occurring in non-human species.
Causes and mechanisms are the clinical question of why a disorder arises, covering immune, infectious, biochemical and physiological explanations.
Immune mechanisms explain disorders through how the defence system recognises, responds, injures or is evaded.
Infectious agents explain disorders through the microbes and viruses that cause them.
Biochemical and physiological mechanisms explain disorders through disturbed molecules, normal function and the systems affected.
Cancer and physiology remainder mechanisms explain what a cancer is at cell and gene level and cover other physiology.
Explanatory fields ask what a disorder is and why it arises by describing its nature and the inherited, infectious or hormonal mechanisms behind it.
Diagnosis and prognosis are the clinical question of how a disorder is detected, identified and its course judged.
Cancer detection fields ask how a cancer is found and what its course is likely to be.
Immune and pathological assessment asks how responses and tissue changes are measured in disease and transplantation.
Detecting fields ask how a disorder is identified through tests, scans, investigative techniques and clinical examination.
Treatment and drugs are the clinical question of how a disorder is managed, by medicines, procedures, therapy and care.
Cancer and immune therapies treat disease by drugs, radiation or manipulation of the immune system.
Drug and biotechnology fields treat disorders with medicines, engineered molecules and cells.
Procedural and specialised treatment fields manage disorders by operation, dental care, general treatment approaches or organ-specific therapy.
Supportive and rehabilitative care restores function and sustains patients in acute and long-term illness.
Alternative approaches address disorders through non-conventional and complementary systems of treatment.
Populations and prevention are the clinical question of how a disorder is distributed, prevented and cared for across groups of people.
Epidemiology and nutrition ask how much disorder exists, who is affected and what diet and exposures contribute.
Patient-group and care-delivery settings ask which people need specialised care and where care is first met.
Health system organisation asks how care is governed, resourced, enabled by technology and kept safe.
Prevention and public health ask how illness is avoided and shaped by society, activity and environment.

fields.name: Mind, brain and society
fields.governing_thought: Mind, brain and society are divided by the unit a claim is about, running from mental processes through nervous systems, persons and interactions to social structures.
fields.note: Worst misplaced: P1.3.5 cognitive psychology under P1.3; P3.3.3.2 sociology of gender and P3.3.4.1 anthropology of gender under persons instead of P5; P1.3.1 genetics under P1.

sections.statement: Mental processes are the unit of claim when psychology studies perception, thought, learning, emotion, awareness and the behaviour they produce.
Human experimental and cognitive topics make claims about how people perceive, move, think, decide and remember.
Motivation, learning and consciousness topics make claims about the internal states that drive and shape mental life.
Behavioural and evolutionary topics make claims about how mind produces behaviour in people, animals and species over evolutionary time.
Nervous systems are the unit of claim when science studies the brain and nerves, their parts, functions and the methods used to measure them.
Whole-field and anatomical topics make claims about the nervous system overall and about its divisions.
Functional, clinical and methodological topics make claims about what the nervous system does, how it fails and how it is recorded or modelled.
Persons are the unit of claim when psychology studies the individual human being across life, personality, health, identity and the discipline itself.
Individual makeup topics make claims about how people differ, change and are measured.
Health and care topics make claims about the disorders, treatments and care settings that affect individual people.
Identity and personal life topics make claims about people as gendered, sexual, relational and named-group beings.
Interactions are the unit of claim when studies concern how people act together in groups, work, communication, law, play and professional service.
Social behaviour and communication topics make claims about how people influence, address and trade with one another.
Work and activity topics make claims about people interacting within jobs, organisations, sport and leisure.
Legal and professional service topics make claims about interactions between practitioners, clients and justice systems.
Social structures are the unit of claim when studies concern institutions, cultures, populations, settings and society as a whole.
Settings and environment topics make claims about the physical and built places in which social life occurs.
Institutions, culture and population topics make claims about the lasting societal forms and demographic patterns of human groups.
Whole-society and boundary topics make claims about how society changes, is theorised and relates to the humanities.

fields.name: Physics
fields.governing_thought: Physics is divided by the scale of the system studied: subatomic, atomic and optical, condensed and soft matter, plasmas and fluids, and gravitational and cosmic.
fields.note: Worst misplaced: P5.1.1.3-P5.1.3.5 (geology, seismology, learning theory under gravity), P2.1.3.1/P2.3.1.4 (network items in atomic), P1.2.3.2-P1.2.3.5 technology under nuclei.

sections.statement: The subatomic scale covers elementary particles, quantum fields and atomic nuclei.
At the subatomic scale, elementary particles and quantum fields form one family of frameworks, species and interactions governed jointly by quantum theory and relativity.
At the subatomic scale, atomic nuclei are studied through their structure, their reactions and decays, and the radiation they produce.
The atomic, molecular and optical scale covers atoms, molecules, light and the quantum probes that resolve them.
At the atomic and molecular scale, atoms and molecules are quantum systems whose structure, collisions and spectra are set by Planck's constant.
At the optical scale, light is studied as rays, waves and quanta, together with the lasers and nonlinear effects that shape it.
At the atomic and optical scale, spectroscopic, absorption and X-ray probes use light and atomic transitions to measure matter precisely.
The condensed and soft matter scale covers many-particle systems: phases, solids, liquids, electronic and magnetic materials, soft, living and network matter.
At the condensed-matter scale, phases and collective statistics describe how very many particles order, transform and behave as liquids, solids and quantum fluids.
At the condensed-matter scale, electronic, magnetic and surface properties of solids and nanostructures govern conduction, order and the devices built from them.
At the soft-matter scale, polymers, granular packings, colloids and living assemblies take their behaviour from huge numbers of weakly bound constituents and thermal energy.
The plasma, fluid and continuum scale covers matter described as a continuous medium: flow, transport, waves, beams and plasmas.
At the continuum scale, plasmas are ionized media whose collective behaviour, fields, radiation and laboratory confinement are treated as one continuous system.
At the continuum scale, charged-particle beams are streams of particles produced, accelerated, transported and used by machines.
At the continuum scale, fluids are liquids and gases treated as continuous media whose flow regimes, media, settings and descriptions follow from fluid dynamics.
At the continuum scale, elastic solids, acoustics and classical electromagnetic fields are continuous media and fields carrying Newtonian motion and waves.
The gravitational and cosmic scale covers gravity, relativity, stars, galaxies and the universe as a whole.
At the gravitational scale, classical gravity, relativity and quantum gravity explain how mass and energy shape spacetime and bulk motion.
At the cosmic scale, planets, stars, galaxies and the universe are observed across wavebands and organised into systems of increasing size.

fields.name: Philosophy
fields.governing_thought: Philosophy is divided by the kind of claim at issue: what there is, how we know and think, how we reason and mean, and what is valuable.
fields.note: Worst: P1.3.1 Philosophy of Action under being, P2.1.4 Epistemology under mind, P4.1.2.3 formal/queer theory under moral value, P2.4.2.3 duplicating mind.

sections.statement: Claims about being ask what exists and what ultimately is, as in metaphysics and the philosophy of religion.
Metaphysics and speculative philosophy cover questions about the fundamental nature of reality and being.
Core theoretical branches of philosophy ask what exists and how we know it.
Topical subfields take up a specific philosophical subject, such as intentional action or religious belief.
Metaphysics of the person and agency asks whether we act freely and what makes us the same person over time.
Claims about knowledge and mind ask how we know and what minds are, as in epistemology, philosophy of mind and consciousness, and the philosophy of the sciences.
Claims about mind ask what minds, cognition and lived experience are and how they are studied psychologically and neurally.
Claims about consciousness ask how awareness appears and how it relates to brain, psychology and physics.
Claims about disordered mind ask how illness and impairment alter awareness, personality and understanding.
Claims about the sciences as ways of knowing ask what grounds the methods and concepts of the sciences and of other disciplines.
Claims about reason and meaning ask what makes inference valid and how language means, as in logic and the philosophy of language.
Logic concepts are fields whose central question is the nature of valid inference and formal reasoning.
Language and interpretation concepts are fields whose central question is how meaning is produced, expressed, and understood in language and texts.
Claims about value ask what is good, right, beautiful and just, as in ethics, aesthetics and political and social philosophy.
Claims about moral value ask what is right and good in professions, life, medicine and technology.
Claims about value in personal relations ask what love and sex are and how they are valued.
Claims about social and political value ask what is just, what rights people hold and how society should be arranged.

fields.name: Politics
fields.governing_thought: Politics is divided by the aspect of power the claim concerns, moving from the source of authority outward through institutions, political behaviour, and policy and administration to relations among states.
fields.note: Misplaced: P3.2.1.3 Polemology and P3.2.1.4 Internationalism (belong in P5), P3.2.4.2 Electoral systems (P2), P3.3.3 Liberalism (P1), P5.4 institutions items (P2/P4).

sections.statement: Authority is the aspect of power concerned with the ideas, ideologies and conditions that found, justify and limit political rule.
Theories and ideologies justify and critique political authority through ideas, beliefs and normative ideals.
Material and economic conditions of power show what shapes authority and who holds it in society.
The scholarly study of power covers the disciplines and methods through which political authority is analysed and taught.
Institutions are the aspect of power concerned with the bodies, offices, regimes and organisations that hold and embody political authority.
Regimes and the state describe the overall forms in which political power is organised.
Governmental and representative bodies are the specific organs through which institutionalised power operates.
Parties, leadership and pluralism are the organised actors and arrangements within institutional politics.
Political behaviour is the aspect of power concerned with how citizens and groups mobilise, participate, contest and resist in pursuit of power.
Participation and opinion cover how citizens and identity groups engage with and are shaped within political life.
Contestation and revolt cover the protest, conflict and upheaval by which groups challenge authority.
Movements and belonging cover the liberation, nationalist and migrant causes through which groups seek recognition and power.
Policy and administration is the aspect of power concerned with how public authority is exercised through governmental bodies in making and carrying out policy.
General administration covers the machinery of government policy-making and implementation across domains.
Sector policies are the domains of governing, covering economy, security, knowledge and social welfare.
Relations among states is the aspect of power concerned with how power is divided, projected and organised across territories, regions and countries.
Federal and territorial division concerns how power is shared among levels of government and contested by regions.
International and imperial relations concern power between states, including empire and independence.
Regional politics concern power as organised in particular countries and regions of the world.
Regional institutions and comparative politics concern how political systems are organised across regions.

fields.name: Religion and theology
fields.governing_thought: Religion and theology are divided by what the inquiry is about: the ultimate and the human condition, authoritative text, practice, and community and institution, moving from the referent to its carriers.
fields.note: P4.2 History of canon law and P4.3 Roman Catholic Church law arguably belong with the law items under P2 (authoritative text).

sections.statement: The ultimate and the human condition is what religious thought is about, including its doctrines, its philosophy and the particular religions that hold beliefs about it.
General inquiry into religion examines belief, myth, doctrine and the philosophy of the ultimate across traditions.
Particular religious traditions each hold a distinct understanding of the ultimate and the human condition.
Authoritative text is what scripture and religious law are about, since both are bodies of writing that carry binding religious authority.
The Bible
Religious law in general. Comparative religious law. Jurisprudence
Jewish law
Islamic law
Practice is what ministry, worship and the lived expression of religion in society and culture are about.
Practical Theology
Religion, society and culture
Worship and ritual are the acts through which believers express and enact their faith together.
Community and institution is what denominations and the church's own governing law are about, as the organised bodies that carry religion.
Christian Denominations
History of canon law
Law of the Roman Catholic Church. The Holy See

fields.name: Strategy
fields.governing_thought: Strategy is divided by the feature of the strategic situation that a claim explains, namely the actors who contend, the game they play, the coercion they apply, the conduct of their operations, and the information each side holds.
fields.note: Misplaced: P4.1.2 Cavalry. Armor duplicates P3.2.2 Armor; P2.3 Peace studies is a discipline, not game structure; P5.2.3 mixes navigation, detection and countermeasures.

sections.statement: Actors are the forces, organisations and personnel that contend in a strategic situation, and their administration and organisation explain who contends.
Military forces and their organisation and administration explain how armed actors are constituted and governed.
Naval and marine personnel are the human actors who crew and serve in naval forces.
The game is the strategic setting of conflict, defence and operational planning that gives the contest its structure.
Conflict and defence research fields are scholarly disciplines that study war, civil conflict and defence as features of the strategic situation.
Conflict Processes
Peace studies
Defense and operations frameworks are the strategic-level arrangements for protecting a population and for planning and conducting military action.
Contemporary security problems are the strategic settings of deterrence, cyber conflict and irregular war.
Coercion is the destructive force that actors apply through weapons, munitions and their physical effects.
Weapon technologies and munitions are the kinds of armament that deliver destructive force against targets.
Combat vehicles, armor, guns and fire control are the land and bombing platforms that bring firepower to bear.
Missile technology and explosive and ballistic science explain how coercive force is launched, travels and detonates.
Conduct is the way actors carry out operations through service branches, supply, maintenance and engineering.
Land combat branches and engineering are the arms through which armies conduct operations.
Logistics, maintenance and support services sustain forces so that operations can continue.
Information is what each side senses, locates, learns and denies, through detection, locating, intelligence and countermeasures.
Detection technologies sense targets through sound, light, radio, magnetic and seismic energy.
Locating, intelligence and countermeasures determine where targets are and exploit or defeat an opponent's detection.
